title: Work came first
text: Yahweh God took the man, and put him into the garden of Eden to cultivate and keep it.
body: Work is in the story before anything goes wrong. It is not part of the curse and it is not a regrettable necessity between weekends — it is what the man was put in the garden to do.

What the fall added was thorns: frustration, futility, the sense of pushing at something that pushes back. That is worth naming, because it means a hard day at work is not evidence that you are in the wrong job or out of God's will.
Both things are true at once. The work is good, and it is hard. A faith that only admits one of those will either romanticise a job or resent it.
question: Do you treat your work as a calling, a cost, or a sentence?
practice: Name one thing your job makes possible for someone else. Say it to God as an offering.
prayer: God, you gave people work before you gave them anything to be sorry for. Let me do mine as yours.

title: The weight in your bag
text: A false balance is an abomination to Yahweh, but accurate weights are his delight.
body: The proverb is about a merchant's scales — the small, unwitnessed adjustment that nobody would ever detect. God's language for it is not disapproval; it is abomination.

The modern equivalents are all small: the hour on the timesheet, the receipt rounded up, the report that leaves one thing out, the sick day that was not. Each is defensible on its own, and that is precisely how integrity goes.
The other half of the verse is easy to miss. Accurate weights are his delight. God is not merely refraining from anger at honest work — he is pleased by it.
question: Which small inaccuracy at work have you stopped noticing?
practice: Correct one of them this week, quietly, even if nobody would ever have known.
prayer: Lord, make my weights accurate when no one is checking.

title: The boss you cannot please
text: with good will doing service, as to the Lord, and not to men; knowing that whatever good thing each one does, he will receive the same again from the Lord, whether he is bound or free.
body: Paul is writing to slaves — people with no leverage, no contract and no way out — and he does not pretend their position is fair. He tells them who their work is actually filed with.
This is not a command to be a doormat. Elsewhere Paul uses every legal right he has. It is a command about the audience: the work goes to God, whatever the man in front of you does with it.
And the promise is specific. Whatever good thing each one does, he will receive the same again — including the parts nobody credited, or credited to somebody else.
question: Whose recognition are you waiting for that is not coming?
practice: Do one piece of work this week deliberately for God, and tell nobody at all.
prayer: Jesus, my work is seen by you even where it is not seen. That is enough.

title: Refusing to be indispensable
text: You shall labor six days, and do all your work, but the seventh day is a Sabbath to Yahweh your God. You shall not do any work in it, you, nor your son, nor your daughter, your male servant, nor your female servant, nor your livestock, nor your stranger who is within your gates;
body: The command covers the household staff and the foreign worker inside the gate, which was radical then and is pointed now. Nobody's rest was to be built on someone else's exhaustion.

Rest is an act of trust. It says the work will hold without me for a day, and that God will keep what I am not currently guarding — which is exactly what a person working far from home finds hardest to believe.
For many, a full day is genuinely not available. Take what is: an evening, a morning, the hours between shifts. The principle is a rhythm, not a loophole to feel guilty about.
question: When did you last stop while things were still undone?
practice: Block a set number of hours this week and do no work in them. Tell one person so it holds.
prayer: God, I am not indispensable and you are not asleep. Teach me to stop.

title: Ready with an answer
text: But sanctify the Lord God in your hearts; and always be ready to give an answer to everyone who asks you a reason concerning the hope that is in you, with humility and fear:
body: Peter assumes the question comes to you. That only happens if something about how you work, wait, or take bad news is visibly different — hope is the thing being asked about.
Ready means having thought about it before you are asked. Most people have never once put into ordinary words why they believe, and so say nothing when a colleague finally asks.
The manner is prescribed as tightly as the content: with humility and fear. An answer delivered as a victory is not the answer Peter means.
question: If a colleague asked you tomorrow why you have hope, what would you actually say?
practice: Write three sentences you could say to a colleague. Keep them plain and true.
prayer: Lord, make the hope in me visible, and make my answer humble when it is asked for.
